prize_parts.citation: For the conception, construction and operation of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening a new window on the cosmic-ray universe

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 statements I keep IceCube (B021) as my preferred single-achievement prize, but with less margin than I claimed before. The discovery is a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos that nobody predicted in detail, found by a decades-long programme (AMANDA, then a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice) and seen in several independent IceCube analysis channels (throughgoing muons, starting events, cascades), with a spectrum and flavour composition that point away from an atmospheric origin. The TXS 0506+056 association in 2017-2018, NGC 1068 and the Galactic-plane map show that real accelerators sit behind it. This is the kind of clue from nature that I think the Committee should reward, and it bears directly on where cosmic rays come from. I stay with a single prize to respect the three-person limit. I keep Halzen, Spiering and Karle: Halzen as the driving scientist, Karle in construction and instrumentation, Spiering as a leader in the collaboration and the analyses that delivered the discovery. Olsson's point that dropping Spiering would weaken the attribution persuades me and I do not change the names.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses have grown clearer. Confirmation of the flux is across IceCube channels, not across detectors, because KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not yet at comparable sensitivity. Source identification rests on a handful of associations at modest significance, so a critic can say the astronomy is early. The three-name cut from a large collaboration and from the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA lineage is a judgement that no one in the committee has shown to be better than another cut. Against that, B014 has six explicit supporters, each with an independent scientific argument, a clean two-name credit and reproduction by several laboratories at the 1e-18 level. I should not mistake my own preference, or the discovery-over-instrument weighting that shapes it, for committee judgement. If the final vote shows that IceCube cannot gather support, I would accept a Katori and Ye prize without reluctance on the science, and the objection I keep is about category, not about quality.

responses.point: Lindroth defends the lattice clock as a real conceptual step (magic wavelength, Lamb-Dicke regime) that tells us something about nature, with agreement at 1e-18 among several laboratories, and names distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as her main reservation.
responses.response: Your argument that the clocks tell us about nature through gravitational time dilation over centimetres and bounds on drifting constants moves me more than I expected, and I withdraw part of my round-1 line that the clock is only a measurement of a world already known. I still see a difference in kind between a discovery that was unpredictable and a technique whose payoff is measured against known physics. You also accept that distinctness from the comb and ion prizes is the open question. Since you have asked whether a one-sentence citation can state it, my reading is that magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a different mechanism from the comb and from single-ion control, so I do not think that objection is fatal. It is why B014 is my first alternative and not a distant second.

responses.point: Kroll argues the lattice clock is a clean two-laureate case of a new measurement technique, independently reproduced, with a payoff in relativistic geodesy, constants and dark-matter searches, and says waiting for the redefinition of the second is not obligatory.
responses.response: Your point that waiting is not obligatory is fair, and I withdraw my earlier suggestion that the clock gains by waiting; the reproduction at 1e-18 does not need the redefinition to make the science secure. We still differ on what the prize is rewarding. You discount your own metrology bias, and I should discount mine toward discoveries. The part of my case that survives is the timing argument for IceCube: its pioneers are alive and active, while the clock will remain an equally strong candidate in later years. I accept that this is an argument about order, not about the merit of the clock.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new class of quantum matter with theory and experiment in one prize, over fifteen years of independent confirmation, and concedes that the credit omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the three-dimensional work, and that B014 is cleaner if the gap is too large.
responses.response: The chair asked each of us what would change our ballot. For you it is the credit gap, and I read your own file as saying that if the gap is large B014 is better. For me B016 has the same difficulty: a prize for the Molenkamp experiment that leaves out the authors of the HgTe proposal it tested, with Zhang deceased, and sits after the 2016 prize on topological phases. I agree with you that the physics is deep and the field is mature, but I do not accept that the credit is clean enough to put it ahead of IceCube or the clock. It stays my second alternative only because I think it may be the strongest candidate in future years, if the committee finds a defensible name set.

responses.point: Pearce moved the lattice clock to the head of his configuration after reading the opening ballots, keeps IceCube as his first alternative, and says independent confirmation by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is thin and the three-person cut is more arbitrary than Katori and Ye.
responses.response: You moved because B014 is the only candidate on which all seven ranking members agree, and you say so openly, which I respect. But I would remind us what the chair summary also says: agreement on B014 is partly the product of members moving toward it, and a count of supporters is not a scientific argument. We agree on the weak points of B021, namely confirmation inside IceCube channels and the arbitrary three-name cut. I still ask for the expert assessment we both mentioned on KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD and on DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA credit before the final ballot. If it shows that independent detectors already corroborate the diffuse flux, I would call the case closed; if it shows the opposite, I would move to B014.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B014 on the basis of the original work (Katori's proposal and demonstration, Ye's record performance), and argues that Spiering must stay in any IceCube credit, since dropping him would weaken the attribution.
responses.response: Thank you for the point about Spiering; I keep the three names Halzen, Spiering and Karle for that reason. Your attention to who did the original work is the right test, and B014 passes it better than B021 does: there is a clear division between concept and realisation in the lattice clock, whereas IceCube credit is spread over a large collaboration. I accept this as the decisive advantage of B014, and it is the reason I name it as my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can obtain an expert assessment of independent confirmation of the diffuse flux from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD, and a historical note on DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA, before the final ballot; my confidence in B021 depends on both.
Whether any three-name cut of the IceCube leadership is defensible against the many others who made decisive contributions; the names are recalled rather than checked.

Whether I weigh the distinction between discovery and instrument too heavily, given that six colleagues give independent scientific arguments for the lattice clock; I may be an outlier for reasons of temperament.
Whether the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes to be stated in one citation sentence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my background is in string theory, quantum gravity and cosmology, and I have no known institutional or collaborative tie to the IceCube, optical lattice clock or topological insulator candidates or their credited names. As Secretary I handle the expert-evaluation requests, which gives me a procedural interest in asking for the assessments I propose, but this is not a conflict on any candidate.
